title: Install the right ASIO driver
summary: ASIO bypasses the Windows audio mixer. The manufacturer's driver is what makes small buffers stable.
steps: Find your interface's model name (on the device or in Device Manager > Sound, video and game controllers).
Download the latest Windows driver from the manufacturer's support page (not from Windows Update or third-party driver sites).
Unplug the interface, install the driver, reboot, then plug it in on the USB port you will keep using.
In your DAW select the manufacturer's ASIO driver, not 'ASIO4ALL', 'Generic Low Latency ASIO' or 'Realtek ASIO'.
No interface yet? FL Studio ASIO (bundled with FL Studio) or ASIO4ALL work with onboard audio, but expect higher latency (10-20 ms).

Drivers of interfaces you no longer own, or entries whose files are missing, only clutter the DAW's driver list and can hang its driver scan: uninstall them in Settings > Apps > Installed apps. If an entry remains, reinstall that driver and uninstall it again.

title: Connect the audio interface properly
summary: Bus-powered interfaces are sensitive to shared, noisy or underpowered USB ports.
steps: Plug the interface directly into a rear motherboard USB port, not into a monitor, keyboard or front-panel hub.
Avoid sharing that USB controller with webcams, external drives or wireless dongles; try a different rear port group if you hear crackles.
If the interface has a power supply, use it, even when it also works on bus power.
Use a short, good-quality cable. If you need a hub, use a powered one.

If you do not apply the USB power tweaks: Device Manager > Universal Serial Bus controllers > each USB Root Hub / hub on the interface's path > Properties > Power Management: untick 'Allow the computer to turn off this device to save power'.
USB 2.0 interfaces work fine in USB 3 ports; prefer ports that are not shared with other high-traffic devices.

title: Windows Sound settings
summary: Things only the Sound control panel can change reliably.
steps: Open the Sound control panel. On the Playback and Recording tabs, open your interface > Properties.
Advanced tab: set the default format to the sample rate you work in (usually 48000 Hz, or 44100 Hz), the same in the DAW.
Advanced tab: decide on 'Allow applications to take exclusive control'. Leave it on if the DAW must grab the device; turn it off if browsers 'steal' the interface.
Enhancements / Audio enhancements: turn them all off (Spatial sound: Off).
Windows 11: Settings > System > Sound > (device) > Audio enhancements: Off. This is per device; check both the playback and the recording device of your interface.
Communications tab: select 'Do nothing' so Windows never ducks audio during calls.
If you have a dedicated interface, consider making onboard audio the Windows default device so system sounds and browsers stay off your DAW interface.

title: BIOS / UEFI settings
summary: Firmware power management and memory settings that Windows cannot change. Menu names vary by board vendor.
steps: Enable XMP / EXPO (memory profile) so RAM runs at its rated speed.
Make sure CPU Turbo / Precision Boost is enabled.
Desktops, only if LatencyMon still shows spikes: try disabling deep C-states (C6/C7, Package C-state) or setting them to 'C1 only'. Costs idle power.
Disable onboard devices you never use (onboard audio if you have an interface, serial ports, extra SATA/RAID controllers, onboard Wi-Fi/Bluetooth on studio-only machines).
Update the BIOS if it is more than about two years old: firmware updates often fix USB and power-management bugs.
After changes, boot into Windows and re-run the scan to compare.

title: Graphics driver
summary: GPU drivers are among the most common sources of DPC spikes (nvlddmkm.sys).
steps: Install the NVIDIA Studio Driver rather than the Game Ready driver; it is tested for stability with creative apps.
During setup choose 'Custom' > 'Perform a clean installation', and only install the Graphics Driver (skip HD Audio if you never use HDMI audio, skip extras).
NVIDIA Control Panel > Manage 3D settings > Power management mode: 'Prefer maximum performance'.
Turn off overlays (NVIDIA app / GeForce Experience overlay, Instant Replay); the tool already disables Xbox Game DVR.

title: Memory Integrity (Core isolation): decide consciously
summary: A real security feature with measurable overhead on some systems. The tool never changes it automatically.
steps: Only consider this if LatencyMon shows high latency after all other steps.
Work or company-managed PC: do not change it; it is likely enforced by policy.
Open Windows Security > Device security > Core isolation details and turn Memory integrity off, then reboot.
Re-test with LatencyMon. If it made no difference, turn it back on.

title: Trim startup apps
summary: RGB, monitoring, sync and game launchers often run polling loops that cause spikes.
steps: Open Settings > Apps > Startup and disable everything you do not need while making music.
Prime suspects: RGB suites (iCUE, Armoury Crate, Aura, SignalRGB, G HUB, Synapse), hardware monitors, cloud sync (OneDrive/Dropbox) on project folders, game launchers.
Pause cloud sync during recording sessions and keep active projects out of synced folders.
Re-run the scan; the background check lists apps it recognises.

title: Keep Windows Update out of your sessions
summary: Updates install drivers and run maintenance in the background.
steps: Set Active hours to cover your usual studio time.
Before an important session or gig: install pending updates and reboot, then use 'Pause updates'.
Under Advanced options, consider turning off 'Receive updates for other Microsoft products' and check that driver updates do not replace your audio interface driver.

title: Laptop specifics
summary: Laptops use aggressive power management that the power plan alone may not override.
steps: Always produce on AC power with the original charger.
Open the vendor control app (Dell Optimizer/Power Manager, Lenovo Vantage, ASUS Armoury Crate, HP Command Center) and select its performance or 'ultra performance' thermal mode.
Set Windows power mode (Settings > System > Power) to 'Best performance'.
Hybrid-GPU laptops: if LatencyMon blames the GPU, try forcing the dedicated GPU (MUX switch / 'dGPU only') in the vendor app or BIOS.

title: Plugins and sample libraries
summary: Where plugins and samples live matters for load times, streaming and stability.
steps: Keep plugin folders (VST3: C:\Program Files\Common Files\VST3, and your VST2 folder) on the internal system SSD.
Put sample libraries on an internal SSD. For Native Instruments/Kontakt libraries use Native Access > Preferences > Content location to move them, so the registry paths stay correct.
External USB drives work for samples, but connect them to a different USB controller than the audio interface and make sure they are connected before the DAW starts.
Replace 32-bit plugins with 64-bit versions; bridged plugins cost CPU and crash more often. Remove plugins you no longer use, the DAW scans every one of them.
Point the DAW's plugin search paths at your real plugin folders, not at whole drives.

title: Verify with LatencyMon
summary: The definitive test: it measures the real worst-case DPC/ISR execution times and names the driver.
steps: Install LatencyMon (free for personal use) from Resplendence.
Close the DAW, press Start (the play button) and use the PC normally for 10-15 minutes: browse, move windows, play audio.
'Your system appears to be suitable for handling real-time audio' = good. Otherwise check the Drivers tab, sort by 'Highest execution (ms)'.

Typical culprits: ndis.sys / wdiwifi.sys / rt640x64.sys (network: disable Wi-Fi, update LAN driver), nvlddmkm.sys / amdkmdag.sys (GPU: clean driver install), ACPI.sys / intelppm.sys (power: BIOS C-states, BIOS update), storport.sys / stornvme.sys (storage), USBPORT.SYS / USBXHCI.SYS (USB: change port or controller).
Apply one fix at a time and re-test, so you know what actually helped.

title: FL Studio audio settings
steps: Device: select your interface's ASIO driver (or 'FL Studio ASIO' with onboard audio).
Click 'Show ASIO panel' and set the buffer: 128-256 samples while recording/playing live, 512-1024 while mixing heavy projects. Use the smallest buffer that plays without underruns.
Sample rate: match the interface and Windows (usually 48000 Hz).
Leave 'Triple buffer' off unless you get underruns that nothing else fixes (it doubles latency). 'Mix in buffer switch' can lower latency on some interfaces but hides underruns from the counter.
Audio processing thread: keep 'Safe overloads' on (otherwise the GUI can freeze during overloads). Raise 'Priority' only if you get underruns; higher values risk lockups.

CPU section: enable 'Multithreaded generator processing', 'Multithreaded mixer processing' and 'Smart disable'. Leave 'Align tick lengths' off; it is a troubleshooting option for plugin clicks or timing drift.

Mixer: 'Resampling' set to 6-point hermite saves CPU during live playback (the default 24-point sinc is fine on fast CPUs). Untick 'Reset plugins on transport' for faster response when jumping around the song.
Playback tracking: Driver. Underruns: watch the counter in Audio settings while playing back a project.

Plugins (Options > Manage plugins): keep the search paths to your real plugin folders, not whole drives. After installing new plugins click 'Find installed plugins' with 'Verify plugins' on and 'Rescan previously verified plugins' off, so only new plugins are scanned.
Large projects: Tools > Macros > 'Switch smart disable for all plugins' to stop idle plugins using CPU.
Optional tweaks in this tool: 'Always start FL Studio with high CPU priority' and the Defender exclusion (includes the Image-Line folders).

title: Cubase audio settings
steps: Audio System: select your interface's ASIO driver (avoid 'Generic Low Latency ASIO Driver' when an interface is connected).
Click the driver entry > Control Panel to set the buffer size: 64-256 samples for recording, larger for mixing.
Audio System: enable 'Activate Steinberg Audio Power Scheme' (keeps the CPU out of power-saving states while Cubase runs).
Enable 'Activate Multi Processing'.
ASIO-Guard: on, level 'Normal' or 'High' for mixing. It adds latency only to tracks that are not record-enabled or monitored.
Studio > Project Setup: sample rate matches the interface.
Use Studio > Audio Performance to see real-time peak vs. average load; real-time peaks point to driver/DPC problems, not CPU power.

title: Nuendo audio settings
summary: Same audio engine as Cubase: Studio > Studio Setup.
steps: Select the interface's ASIO driver and set the buffer in its Control Panel.
Enable 'Activate Steinberg Audio Power Scheme' and 'Activate Multi Processing'.
ASIO-Guard on (Normal/High) for mixing sessions.

title: Ableton Live audio settings
steps: Driver Type: ASIO. Audio Device: your interface.
Hardware Setup opens the driver panel; set Buffer Size there (128-256 recording, 512+ mixing).
Sample rate: match Windows and the interface.
CPU tab (Live 11/12): make sure multicore support is on.
Use 'Reduced Latency When Monitoring' only while tracking.

title: REAPER audio settings
steps: Audio system: ASIO, then your interface's driver; set the block size in 'ASIO Configuration...'.
Audio > Buffering: keep 'Anticipative FX processing' enabled (multi-core rendering ahead of time).
Audio > Buffering: thread priority 'Highest (recommended)'.
Disable 'Close audio device when stopped' if devices take long to reopen.

title: Bitwig Studio audio settings
steps: Driver model: ASIO, device: your interface.
Set block size (128-256 tracking, 512+ mixing) and match the sample rate.
Settings > Plug-ins: 'Together' or 'By manufacturer' hosting uses fewer resources than 'Individually'; use 'Individually' only to isolate crashing plugins.

title: Studio One audio settings
steps: Audio Device: your interface's ASIO driver.
Device Block Size: 128-256 for recording. Enable 'Dropout Protection' (Medium/High) for mixing, and 'Native Low-Latency Monitoring' for tracking.
Process Precision: Single (64-bit only if needed).

title: Pro Tools audio settings
summary: Setup > Playback Engine and Setup > Hardware.
steps: Playback Engine: select your interface's ASIO driver.
H/W Buffer Size: 64-256 for recording, 1024 for mixing.
Enable Dynamic Plug-In Processing; adjust Host Processors to the number of cores minus one or two.
